Healthleap raises $38M for AI that finds undiagnosed conditions in hospital patients
Nickie Louise
Posted On October 7, 2026
0
4.4K Views
0
Shares
Share On Facebook
Tweet It
Malnutrition is one of the most common conditions hiding in plain sight inside U.S. hospitals. Up to half of hospitalized patients may be at risk, according to Healthleap, but fewer than 9% receive a diagnosis. That gap can mean longer hospital stays, worse patient outcomes, and millions of dollars in added costs.
Healthleap thinks software can catch what busy clinical teams miss.
The healthcare AI startup has raised $38 million in combined seed and Series A funding to expand a platform that reads patient records daily and flags people who may be at risk for undetected conditions. The financing includes an $8 million seed round co-led by Sequoia Capital and First Round Capital and a $30 million Series A led by Hummingbird Ventures.
Healthleap’s story started with malnutrition. Co-founder Jemima Meyer was working as a clinical dietitian when she built an early tool to help dietitians find patients who needed attention sooner. She later teamed up with her brother, Josiah Meyer, and the pair founded Healthleap in South Africa in 2022.
What began as a nutrition tool has since become a broader clinical AI platform. Healthleap now sits on top of hospital electronic health record systems, analyzing notes, lab results, vital signs, medications, diagnoses and other patient data for signs that someone may need a closer look.
The software does not diagnose patients. It assigns risk scores and routes them into existing hospital workflows so clinicians can decide what happens next.
From malnutrition screening to a broader hospital AI layer
Healthleap’s pitch is gaining attention partly because the company can point to measurable results.
At the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, Healthleap says its malnutrition program generated $23.8 million in annualized financial impact. That figure included $6.3 million in additional reimbursement and an estimated $17.5 million tied to shorter hospital stays, representing 8,632 annualized bed-days saved. Penn Medicine’s Strategic Decision Support team reviewed the analysis, Healthleap said.
At Cedars-Sinai, the company reports a 39% increase in malnutrition diagnoses with the same staffing levels and $11 million in annual financial impact.
Announcing the funding in a LinkedIn post, Josiah said :
“Somewhere right now, a patient is getting sicker from something that was treatable all along. HealthLeap AI finds these patients. We use existing signals in the patient record to screen every inpatient every day and flag those at high risk, so care teams can act and care for those patients. We started with malnutrition. My sister and co-founder, Jemima, worked as a clinical dietitian and watched patients get found too late.”
Healthleap also has clinical research behind its core malnutrition model. A peer-reviewed study published in *Applied Clinical Informatics* evaluated more than 166,000 hospital admissions over 3.75 years

articles.text:
ZAP Surgical Raises $36 Million Led By Catalio Capital To Scale Non-Invasive Brain Surgery
By Amit Chowdhry
Oct 19, 2026
ZAP Surgical Raises $36 Million Led By Catalio Capital To Scale Non-Invasive Brain Surgery
ZAP Surgical Systems has secured $36 million in financing led by Catalio Capital Management, with continued support from Baheal, the company’s strategic partner in China. The funding will support the global expansion of ZAP’s non-invasive robotic brain surgery platform and continued development of its technology across neuroscience applications.
ZAP develops the ZAP-X Gyroscopic Radiosurgery platform, a vault-free radiosurgery system designed for non-invasive treatment of brain tumors and other neurological conditions. The company recently shipped its 50th ZAP-X system and is increasing production capacity to support growing demand from academic medical centers, community hospitals, and physician-led practices.
Nearly 10,000 patients have been treated worldwide using ZAP-X, according to the company. The new financing will help ZAP broaden commercial adoption in the United States and other international markets while expanding manufacturing and deployment capacity.
Catalio Capital Management led the round as part of its healthcare and AI investment strategy. Nicholas von Guionneau, M.D., Ph.D., of Catalio is also joining ZAP’s board as an observer.
Beyond its established work in neuro-oncology, ZAP is studying an emerging approach it calls radiomodulation, which uses precisely targeted low-dose ionizing radiation with the goal of influencing neurological activity. The company and its collaborators have evaluated the concept in multiple mammalian brain models over the past decade.
ZAP recently reported preliminary findings from a first-in-human pilot study evaluating radiomodulation delivered with the ZAP-X platform in patients with severe treatment-resistant depression. The company characterized the early results as encouraging and said broader multicenter studies are being planned, beginning with treatment-resistant depression and addiction. These neuropsychiatric applications remain investigational, and additional clinical research will be required to establish safety and efficacy.
Founded in 2014 by neurosurgeon John R. Adler, M.D., ZAP is focused on expanding access to non-invasive robotic therapeutics in neuroscience. Adler is Emeritus Dorothy & TK Chan Professor of Neurosurgery and Radiation Oncology at Stanford University.
Baheal has supported ZAP’s expansion in China, while Catalio’s investment is expected to help accelerate U.S. adoption and broader international growth.
KEY QUOTES:
“This financing reflects our conviction that ZAP Surgical is uniquely positioned to usher in a new wave of non-invasive radiosurgery globally. With rising healthcare costs in developed nations and underserved populations in emerging markets, intelligent robotics will play an indispensable role in reducing cost structures while elevating the standard of care. ZAP’s mission to make non-invasive brain therapy broadly accessible aligns perfectly with our strategy of backing disruptive healthcare technologies.”
Nicholas von Guionneau, M.D., Ph.D., Catalio Capital Management

articles.text:
D2 Capital Advisors Arranges $35.83 Million Construction Financing For Somerset Phase II In Philadelphia
By Amit Chowdhry
Oct 13, 2026
D2 Capital Advisors Arranges $35.83 Million Construction Financing For Somerset Phase II In Philadelphia
D2 Capital Advisors arranged and closed a $35.83 million construction financing package for Somerset Phase II, a 170-unit multifamily development at 2202 E. Somerset Street in Philadelphia’s Port Richmond neighborhood.
The project is the next phase of Riverwards Group’s Somerset Station master plan.
The financing package includes a $19.87 million senior construction loan from Silver Heights Capital and $15.96 million in Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy financing from Nuveen Green Capital.
D2 Capital Advisors arranged both tranches on behalf of Riverwards Group, which is led by principals Mo Rushdy and Larry McKnight, P.E., LEED-GA.
The two financing components will fund construction of the 146,158-square-foot project.
Somerset Phase II will include 76 studio apartments, 38 one-bedroom units, and 56 two-bedroom units, along with on-site garage parking.
The development also benefits from a grandfathered 10-year, 100% real estate tax abatement.
Urban Renewal Builders, Riverwards Group’s affiliated general contractor, is constructing the project.
Both the senior loan and the C-PACE financing were structured on a non-recourse basis.
Combined with more than $10 million in sponsor equity, the financing supports a total project cost of approximately $46 million.
The transaction was led by Jack Cortese and David Frankel of D2 Capital Advisors.
The team structured the layered senior debt and C-PACE financing with the goal of maximizing proceeds while reducing Riverwards Group’s overall cost of capital.
Somerset Phase II is located next to the 220-unit first phase of Somerset Station.
Phase I is complete and fully occupied and was sold to the Philadelphia Housing Authority in May 2025 for $58.1 million.
The new financing fully funds another 170 units, which are expected to be delivered in early 2028.
The project is also expected to position the broader Somerset Station master plan for a future third phase.
Riverwards Group has operated across Philadelphia’s Riverwards neighborhoods since 2009 and has delivered more than 1,500 homes and multifamily units.
Its portfolio includes Somerset Station, Kensington Courts, Avenue V, N5 Square, and The Lenora.
D2 Capital Advisors has arranged more than $1.25 billion in financings nationwide across commercial real estate asset classes.
KEY QUOTES:
“Somerset Phase II shows what a proven sponsor and a proven site can do for a financing. Riverwards built Phase I on this same site, delivered it, and sold it to the Philadelphia Housing Authority, so Silver Heights and Nuveen were underwriting a team and a product that had already delivered here. Layer in a thinning supply pipeline ahead of an early 2028 delivery, and we were able to put together a $35.8 million capital stack that fits the business plan and sets Riverwards up well for what comes next at Somerset Station.”
Jack Cortese, D2 Capital Advisors
“We completed significant site work at the property during Phase I, so Phase II was positioned for vertical construction to begin quickly.
